title: Election Commission Fixes Website Flaw That Exposed Voter Data, Reuters Finds
excerpt: A call-booking feature on the ECI website leaked voters' personal details and identity-document file paths through predictable form reference numbers. Reuters alerted the commission on October 26; the flaw was fixed within hours on Thursday.
body:
• A flaw on the Election Commission of India's website exposed some voters' names, phone numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, home addresses and file paths to identity documents they had uploaded, Reuters found.
  • The weakness sat in a call-booking feature introduced in June 2025: form reference numbers visible in a browser's network tab followed a predictable pattern, which researchers said could have let hackers guess numbers and download data in bulk.
  • Reuters alerted the ECI on October 26; the commission did not respond for a month, then fixed the flaw within hours on Thursday after its spokesman said the IT division had been asked to look into the findings.
  • Reuters could not determine whether the flaw was ever exploited, how long it existed, or how many voters were affected.

A security flaw in India's Election Commission (ECI) website that was allowing access to sensitive personal details and documents of some voters has been fixed, after Reuters discovered the vulnerability and alerted the institution. Researchers who reviewed the findings said the flaw could have been easily abused.

How the flaw worked

A Reuters review over more than a month of the ECI's website showed that when a voter logged into their account and requested a telephone call with their local electoral officer, the network tab in an ordinary browser's developer tools — opened with a simple right click — started showing the reference number of the form the voter had submitted online to enrol or update their information. Using those reference numbers to book the call, the same network details then revealed personal information such as the user's name, phone number, email, date of birth and address, and even file paths to identification documents like passports that had been submitted. The details were not visible on the browser's main screen, which pointed to a vulnerability in the website's code, Indian security researchers Karan Saini and Ehraz Ahmed told Reuters after reviewing the findings step by step.

The bigger concern, the researchers said, was that the reference numbers followed a predictable pattern, meaning hackers could guess them and automate downloads of large amounts of data. The call-booking feature in which Reuters detected the flaw was introduced in June 2025.

A month of silence, then a same-day fix

Reuters first shared its findings and sought comment from the ECI and its three commissioners on October 26, but they did not respond despite repeated requests. On Thursday, an ECI spokesman said the commission's information technology division had been asked to look into the findings. Hours later, the vulnerability was fixed, with sensitive fields — including personal details and file paths — redacted, according to a Reuters review. The two researchers confirmed the fix effectively blocked any abuse of the data, as Deccan Herald's report of the Reuters investigation also records.

What remains unknown

Reuters could not determine whether the flaw had been exploited, how long it had existed, or how many voters could have been affected — and the ECI has not said. That gap matters because of the data involved: names and addresses paired with dates of birth, phone numbers and identity-document file paths are the raw material for impersonation and targeted fraud, which is why the researchers treated predictable reference numbers as the most serious part of the finding.

Why the timing is sensitive

The security issue, and the fix, come months ahead of elections in key Indian states, including the most populous, Uttar Pradesh, and while the ECI is facing growing public anger over a contentious drive to update voter lists. The ECI says it has complied with all regulations, while the BJP argues opposition groups are misleading the country after failing to win elections. For voters, the immediate position is that the specific exposure Reuters demonstrated is closed; whether any data left the system before the fix is a question only the commission's own logs can answer, and it has not addressed it publicly.
nri_angle: NRIs who enrol or update voter details through the ECI portal are among the users whose submitted identity documents passed through the affected feature.
author: Diaspora Desk
